The proportion of patients whose alert was available at the next anaesthetic ranged from 45 to 80 percent, and combined systems performed better than single tools. Only four studies measured whether the next anaesthetist actually saw the alert before airway management, and none measured patient harm. Most were single-centre before-after comparisons without adjustment for concurrent airway initiatives."},{"title":"Wristband alerts for known difficult airway: a before-after study in a teaching hospital","authors":"Castellano-Brightwell J, Oyelaran-Frost M","year":2019,"venue":"Anaesthesia Practice and Safety","doi":"10.5555/aps.2019.0317","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After introducing a coloured wristband for inpatients with a documented difficult airway, we compared 18 months before and after. The proportion of patients whose known difficulty was documented as recognised before their next anaesthetic rose from 38 to 71 percent. Recognition was lowest for emergency airway management outside theatres. A new electronic record was introduced during the after period, and staff training on airway alerts ran at the same time, so the change cannot be attributed to the wristband alone."},{"title":"Visibility of electronic difficult airway alerts to anaesthetists before induction: an observational study","authors":"Nakashima-Doyle F, Petrov-Asante L, Whitcombe-Obi R","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Airway Management Research","doi":"10.5555/jamr.2022.0288","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined 412 subsequent anaesthetics in patients with an electronic difficult airway alert in two hospitals. The alert was displayed in the anaesthetic record in 88 percent of cases, but documented as read before induction in only 54 percent. Alerts were missed more often out of hours and when the patient was transferred from another hospital. Anaesthetists reported alert fatigue from other electronic warnings. Documentation of reading the alert may underestimate how often it was actually seen. Alerts were displayed less often for patients transferred in, because records from other hospitals did not carry them."},{"title":"Unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation after a documented difficult airway: frequency and consequences","authors":"Lindqvist-Mahlangu T, Ferreira-Kowalski D","year":2020,"venue":"Anaesthesia Practice and Safety","doi":"10.5555/aps.2020.0409","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In a regional database of 2,030 patients with a documented difficult tracheal intubation, we reviewed the next airway management within five years. Difficulty was unanticipated in 31 percent of cases, and unanticipated cases more often involved multiple attempts, desaturation below 80 percent and emergency front-of-neck access. Unanticipated difficulty was commoner in emergency settings and in patients treated at a different hospital from the index event. The database relied on voluntary reporting and probably missed some events. Patients whose difficulty was unanticipated were more often older and admitted as emergencies."},{"title":"Do patients know? Awareness of difficult airway status and use of alert letters","authors":"Achebe-Morrison S, Tanaka-Whitlock J","year":2023,"venue":"Patient Safety in Perioperative Care","doi":"10.5555/pspc.2023.0074","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We telephoned 180 patients who had been sent a difficult airway letter between 6 and 36 months earlier. Forty percent could say that they had a difficult airway and 22 percent reported carrying the letter or an alert card. Awareness was lower in older patients, patients with limited English and patients whose index anaesthetic had been an emergency. Several patients said the letter used technical language they did not understand. The response rate was 61 percent. Patients who had discussed the letter with their GP were more likely to know their status."},{"title":"Using a hospital difficult airway database for research: completeness and linkage to later anaesthetics","authors":"Brennan-Oyelowo P, Suzuki-Hartmann E","year":2018,"venue":"Perioperative Data and Informatics","doi":"10.5555/pdi.2018.0023","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared a hospital's difficult airway database with a manual review of anaesthetic records over two years. The database captured 76 percent of events meeting its own definition, with lower capture for events outside theatres. Linkage of database entries to later anaesthetics in the same hospital succeeded for 90 percent using the hospital number. Anaesthetics in other hospitals were invisible to the database. The authors recommend reporting capture rates alongside any outcome derived from such databases. Capture improved after a reporting prompt was added to the anaesthetic record in the second year."},{"title":"Interrupted time series for evaluating hospital safety interventions: pitfalls with few data points and concurrent changes","authors":"Okafor-Linde R, Delacroix-Bhatt S","year":2024,"venue":"Quality and Safety Methods","doi":"10.5555/qsm.2024.0012","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We re-analysed 42 published interrupted time series of hospital safety interventions. Twenty-six had fewer than eight data points on one side of the change, and 19 did not mention concurrent interventions. Re-analysis with autocorrelation and seasonality taken into account changed the conclusion in 11 studies. We recommend at least eight points before and after, a pre-specified model, a control series where possible, and an explicit list of co-interventions with their dates. Studies with a control series were less likely to change conclusion on re-analysis, but only five of the 42 used one."}]}
